title: The New Deal
summary: Franklin D. Roosevelt crushed Herbert Hoover in 1932 amid the worst of the Great Depression, and his first three months in office—the Hundred Days—produced a burst of legislation unmatched in American history. After declaring a bank holiday, FDR rescued the banking system and created federal deposit insurance. A wave of new agencies followed: the NRA drafted industry codes for prices and wages, the AAA paid farmers to cut production, the CCC and PWA put the jobless to work, and the TVA brought flood control and cheap public electricity to a poor southern region. This experimental First New Deal eased the crisis but did not end it, and in 1935–1936 a conservative Supreme Court struck down both the NRA and the AAA.

Pressure from below pushed Roosevelt further left. A massive labor upheaval produced the CIO, which organized whole industries and won recognition from General Motors through the Flint sit-down strike, while Huey Long, Francis Townsend, and Father Coughlin demanded bolder redistribution of wealth. The Second New Deal of 1935 shifted the emphasis from recovery to economic security: the WPA employed millions, the Wagner Act guaranteed workers the right to unionize, and the Social Security Act built an American welfare state of old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and aid to dependent families. FDR's 1936 landslide cemented a durable New Deal coalition, and although his court-packing scheme failed, the justices stopped invalidating economic regulation. A sharp 1937 recession pushed the administration toward Keynesian deficit spending before a conservative coalition in Congress halted further reform.

The New Deal redefined liberalism and linked freedom to economic security, but its benefits were unequal. To hold southern votes, Social Security excluded agricultural and domestic workers—the jobs most Black Americans held—while FHA redlining deepened housing segregation and the AAA displaced tenant farmers. Women were channeled toward the least generous programs, hundreds of thousands of Mexican-Americans were pressured to leave the country, and the Indian Reorganization Act reversed forced assimilation without ending reservation poverty. Even so, Black voters shifted to the Democrats, and Popular Front culture celebrated a pluralist, worker-centered Americanism. Unemployment persisted until World War II mobilization finally ended the Depression.
big_ideas: The New Deal transformed the meaning of American liberalism from limited government into active federal responsibility for citizens' economic security.
The First New Deal (1933) stressed relief and recovery through experimental agencies, while the Second New Deal (1935) built lasting guarantees of security such as Social Security and the Wagner Act.
Grassroots movements—the CIO's industrial unionism, Huey Long's Share Our Wealth, and the Townsend plan—pushed Roosevelt toward bolder reform.
After the failed court-packing plan of 1937, the Supreme Court permanently accepted federal regulation of the economy, a lasting constitutional shift.
The New Deal coalition of workers, farmers, urban ethnics, northern Black voters, and the white South realigned American politics for decades.

New Deal benefits flowed unevenly: the 'southern veto' excluded most Black workers from Social Security, FHA redlining entrenched housing segregation, and women were steered into stigmatized public assistance.
Despite enormous change, the New Deal never ended mass unemployment; only World War II production did.

key_terms.def: FDR's sweeping program of relief, recovery, and reform launched in 1933 to fight the Great Depression, which permanently enlarged the federal government's role in the economy.
The remarkably productive opening months of FDR's presidency in spring 1933, when Congress passed fifteen major laws creating the core agencies of the First New Deal.
A 1933 agency that had business leaders write codes governing prices, output, and wages; dominated by big firms and declared unconstitutional in the 1935 Schechter case.
A 1933 law that raised crop prices by paying farmers to produce less; it helped landowners but pushed tenants and sharecroppers off the land, and the Court voided it in 1936.
A work-relief program that put millions of young men to work on reforestation, flood control, and park projects for modest government wages.
A federal agency that built dams along the Tennessee River to control floods and sell cheap public electricity, putting the government in direct competition with private utilities.
The drought-stricken southern Plains of the mid-1930s, where over-plowed soil blew away in massive storms, driving more than a million farm families to migrate, many to California.
A New Deal agency that insured long-term, low-down-payment mortgages, making homeownership widely affordable, but its refusal to back loans in minority neighborhoods reinforced segregation.
The labor federation founded by John L. Lewis in 1935 to organize all workers in mass-production industries such as autos and steel, rather than by separate crafts.
A tactic in which strikers occupied their factories to prevent replacement workers; the UAW used it at GM's Flint plants in 1936–1937 to win union recognition.
Louisiana senator Huey Long's 1934 plan to confiscate great fortunes and guarantee every family an income; its popularity pressured FDR toward the Second New Deal before Long's 1935 assassination.
The Second New Deal's giant jobs program, which employed about three million people a year building roads, bridges, and airports and funding artists, writers, and theater.
The 1935 National Labor Relations Act, which created a federal board to supervise union elections and banned employer practices like firing organizers, giving labor real legal protection.
The 1935 centerpiece of the Second New Deal, establishing old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and aid to the disabled and dependent children—the foundation of the American welfare state.
FDR's 1937 proposal to add justices to the Supreme Court to protect New Deal laws; Congress rejected it, but the Court soon began upholding economic regulation anyway.
Commissioner John Collier's reforms, including the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act, which ended land allotment and forced assimilation and restored a measure of tribal self-government.

timeline.event: Nine Black youths are arrested in the Scottsboro case, which becomes an international civil rights cause.
Franklin D. Roosevelt wins the presidency in a landslide, promising a 'new deal' for the American people.
The Hundred Days produce the Emergency Banking Act, NRA, AAA, CCC, and TVA; the Twenty-first Amendment ends Prohibition.
Huey Long launches Share Our Wealth as roughly 2,000 strikes sweep the country; the Dust Bowl intensifies on the Plains.
The Second New Deal creates the WPA, Wagner Act, and Social Security; the Supreme Court voids the NRA; the CIO is organized.
The Court strikes down the AAA, FDR wins reelection with over 60 percent of the vote, and Keynes publishes his General Theory.
The Flint sit-down strike wins UAW recognition from GM; FDR's court-packing plan fails, but the Court begins upholding New Deal laws; a sharp recession hits.
The Fair Labor Standards Act sets a national minimum wage and bans child labor in interstate commerce; HUAC is established.
Eleanor Roosevelt arranges Marian Anderson's Lincoln Memorial concert after the DAR bars her from Constitution Hall.
With reform stalled by a conservative coalition, unemployment still exceeds 15 percent as attention turns to war in Europe.

themes: Politics and power: The New Deal vastly expanded federal authority over banking, agriculture, labor, and welfare, and forged a Democratic coalition that dominated politics for decades.
Work, exchange, and technology: Industrial unionism, federal wage-and-hour regulation, and public projects like the TVA and rural electrification reshaped the American economy and workplace.
American and national identity: New Deal programs redefined citizenship around economic security, yet race and gender exclusions showed the boundaries of that promise.

Migration and settlement: The Dust Bowl uprooted a million farm families, AAA policies displaced sharecroppers, and pressured 'repatriation' pushed hundreds of thousands of Mexican-Americans out of the country.
Geography and environment: Massive dam and conservation projects transformed regions like the Tennessee Valley and Columbia River basin, with both economic benefits and ecological costs.
